title: "Day 3 – The methods and your report"

The third day teaches the methods behind the analyses of the second day, as taught sessions on the data of the case: the country-year panel first, then the respondents within the country-years, and then the same model stated as a posterior distribution. Each session has a module of the companion curriculum as its reading, before or after the session. The afternoon turns the analysis that you declared in Task 5 into a short report, written in Quarto and kept under Git.

## 1. Panel data

The country-year panel and the linear model, clustered standard errors, fixed effects in their two designs and what each absorbs, standard errors when 27 countries carry all the evidence, random effects, and the within–between model, which separates the variation within a country over time from the differences between countries.

[Open the slides](../../slides/eu-frames-panel-data.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Read Panel data](../../companion/panel-data.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 2. Multilevel models and the respondents

The same models in the vocabularies of sociology, political science, econometrics and psychology, set side by side; respondents in countries, random intercepts and random slopes; individual effects against aggregate associations; and the model of the original author (OA) fitted at the level of the respondents. In the workspace, `prep/01_build_respondents.R` builds the file of respondents from the Eurobarometer waves that you downloaded, the file on which the person-level models of the module were fitted.

[Open the slides](../../slides/eu-frames-multilevel.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Read Multilevel models](../../companion/multilevel.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 3. Bayesian estimation

The model of the claim stated as a posterior distribution: priors and what they imply, partial pooling across countries, the uncertainty of a result with few clusters, and the checks that a Bayesian workflow runs before a posterior is read.

[Open the slides](../../slides/eu-frames-bayesian.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Read Bayesian estimation](../../companion/bayesian.qmd){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

## 4. Your report

[Open the slides](../../slides/eu-frames-report.qmd){.btn .btn-primary target="_blank"} [Open Git and GitHub](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/git-github.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"} [Open Quarto documents](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/quarto.html){.btn .btn-outline-primary target="_blank"}

Open the workspace in your IDE and turn its folder into a repository, with the preregistration block that you completed in Task 5 as the first commit. Then write the report around the declared analysis: the result with its uncertainty under the errors that you declared, its place on the curve of the claim, any departure from the declaration and the reason for it, and what the replication with new data adds. Render the report from a clean session, and commit each step with a message that says what changed. The modules on Git and GitHub and on Quarto documents hold the steps, and publishing the rendered report is an option for the end of the day. Keep the file of respondents out of the repository: the workspace ignores it, and the terms of GESIS do not allow it to be shared.

**By the end of the day** you can say what each estimator of the menu compares and assumes, at the level of the country-year and of the respondent, and you have a report of your own whose history shows the declaration before the result.
